evals.name: checkout-sequence
evals.prompt: Can you map out how our checkout actually works? Browser posts to our Go API, we write the order row in Postgres, call Stripe to authorize, then send a receipt through Postmark. I keep losing track of what happens when Stripe declines.
evals.expected_output: A single sequence diagram in mermaid with the failure path modelled, the external calls marked as costing money, and a short note on what it deliberately omits.
assertions: Emits a mermaid sequenceDiagram (not a flowchart) as the primary view
Models the decline path explicitly, using an alt/else fragment rather than only the happy path
Marks or notes the calls that cross to an external paid service
Keeps participants to roughly five or fewer
States what the view deliberately omits, or which question it answers, rather than presenting it as a complete description of the system

evals.name: unit-cost-of-a-feature
evals.prompt: We charge 19 EUR/month flat and just launched an AI summary feature. Each summary sends about 6k tokens in and 800 out, does three DB queries, writes a 200KB file, and roughly 1 in 100 generates a support ticket that takes ~6 minutes. Some users generate hundreds a month. Is this going to hurt us?
evals.expected_output: A per-driver cost table, contribution and break-even usage per subscriber, the dominant driver named, rates flagged as needing lookup, and the heavy-tail warning about averages.
assertions: Produces a per-driver cost table covering inference, support, and infrastructure separately
Names the dominant cost driver explicitly and points optimisation at it
Computes a break-even usage per subscriber from the monthly price
Flags model/infra rates as needing to be looked up rather than asserting current provider prices as fact
Warns that usage is heavy-tailed so the average subscriber is not the design input, and asks for or reasons about the distribution

evals.name: order-lifecycle
evals.prompt: Our order status field has nine values: draft, placed, paid, payment_failed, shipped, delivered, cancelled, refunded, expired. Nobody knows which transitions are legal and we've shipped two bugs from it. Help.
evals.expected_output: A state machine in mermaid covering all nine states with triggers and guards, timeouts modelled as transitions, illegal transitions named explicitly, and terminal states identified.
assertions: Emits a mermaid stateDiagram-v2 covering all nine named states
Gives transitions a trigger, and a guard where the transition is conditional
Models at least one timeout or expiry as an explicit transition rather than leaving it implicit
Names at least one illegal transition that should be impossible by construction
Identifies the terminal states, and shows every non-terminal state having an exit
